summary.text: 北 is written today for “north.” Its ancient form is interpreted as two people turned back-to-back; the graph was used for “north” as a sound-based loan in Shang-period writing. The proposed earlier sense involving turning one’s back is not securely attested, and its connection to “north” remains a hypothesis.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph depicts two human figures turned away from each other. The Shang-period use for “north” is a separate whole-graph loan, not a meaning shown by the picture. The proposed original word meaning “turn against” or “back on” is an interpretation of the image, not a securely attested earliest meaning.

components.text: 北 is treated here as an indivisible pictograph: its paired strokes depict two people facing away from each other. No separate modern component or sound element is established by the evidence.

history.text: Oracle-bone and later script examples are reported, and the back-to-back conception is described as continuing through the seal-script form, with changes in stroke execution. The curated oracle-style and seal-style images are modern redrawings that illustrate these reported forms; they are not artifact photographs and do not establish a detailed sequence of intermediate changes.

The Han dictionary also analyzes the graph as two people back-to-back and gives a gloss interpreted as “turning away” or “contrary.” This records a Han-period account, not independent proof of the graph’s earliest use.

Around the Qin–Han transition, 北 was still used for the word “back” as 背 began to distinguish that word in writing. 背 combines 肉, the flesh element, with 北 as a sound element; by the Eastern Han, 背 was reportedly the usual graph for “back.” This is a change in written practice, not evidence that the spoken word began then.

uncertainties.text: The proposed original sense “turn against” or “turn one’s back” is inferred from the graphic conception and later uses; the study reports no secure excavated example writing that hypothesized sense. The evidence does not establish the exact chronology of the proposed senses or every semantic link between them.

The graph is reported as a loan for “north” from Shang-period use, but the proposed relation between “back” and “north” is not directly demonstrated. The old word or object-name behind the graph’s proposed sound match is not recoverable from this evidence; the account proposes that a similar-sounding word allowed the sign to be reused, rather than showing that “north” developed in meaning from “back.”

senses.period: Shang period onward (reported); exact first occurrence not established here
senses.text: The study reports 北 used for the direction “north” as a loan from Shang-period writing, and says this became its principal continuing function. The dossier does not supply a directly inspected inscription context for a named earliest occurrence.

senses.gloss: turn against; turn one’s back on
senses.text: This is a proposed earlier word associated with the back-to-back image and the Han dictionary gloss. Secure excavated examples writing this sense are not identified in the study.

senses.period: Qin–Han manuscripts attest the written use; spoken-sense chronology unresolved
senses.text: 北 was used to write the word “back”; 背 later became the usual graph. This graph differentiation does not establish when the spoken word arose or prove a semantic path from “turn against.”

senses.period: Qin–Han written examples reported; exact chronology unresolved
senses.text: The study reports written examples of 北 for “back side.” Their attestation does not by itself establish when the spoken sense developed or its precise relation to other proposed senses.

developments.text: A semantic connection is proposed, but the earlier sense is not securely attested and the written examples do not establish the chronology of spoken meanings.

The reported Shang-period use for “north” is explained as reuse of the graph for a different word because of a proposed sound similarity. The source-word name and sound comparison are unavailable here, so the borrowing mechanism remains an etymological proposal; it is not a demonstrated meaning change from “back” to “north.”

limitations.text: The dossier reports Shang-period use for “north” but does not provide a directly inspected full inscription context for a specific earliest example. It also cannot establish the hypothesized original sense or the exact order and links among the proposed meanings.

overview.text: 北 means “north.” Its ancient form is interpreted as two people turned back-to-back. The graph was reportedly reused for “north” because of a proposed sound similarity, though the older word and exact sound match are not established here.

components.text: Read the graph as one paired picture: two people turned away from each other. The proposed older “turn against” sense is an interpretation, not a securely attested earliest meaning.

takeaway.text: “North” is explained as a sound-based loan, not as a meaning that clearly developed from “back.”
